LEXASSIST LEGAL QA — CRIMINAL LAW
============================================================

Q: How did the Supreme Court of India rule on the appeal against the AFT's decision?
A: The Supreme Court of India upheld the AFT's decision and dismissed the appeal, affirming that Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly was entitled to the promotion as DGMS (Army).
Case: Union of India vs. Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly
Date: 1st August 2018

---

Q: Why did the High Court of Madras at Madurai Bench set aside the final decree passed by the trial court in the case Selvi vs. Gopalakrishnan Nair (D) Thr. LRs. and Ors.?
A: The High Court set aside the final decree because it held that the appellant/plaintiff could not lay a claim to Survey No.988, which the first respondent/second defendant claimed belonged to him.
Case: Selvi vs. Gopalakrishnan Nair (D) Thr. LRs. and Ors.
Date: 15th May 2018

---

Q: On what grounds did the High Court of Delhi affirm the decision to reject the plaint in the case Shakti Bhog Food Industries Ltd. vs. The Central Bank of India & Anr.?
A: The High Court of Delhi affirmed the decision to reject the plaint on the grounds that the suit was filed beyond the limitation period specified under Article 113 of the Limitation Act, 1963, which is three years from the date when the right to sue accrued.
Case: Shakti Bhog Food Industries Ltd. vs. The Central Bank of India & Anr.
Date: 5th June 2020

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court decide regarding the pending litigations between Anu Bhandari and Pradip Bhandari?
A: The Supreme Court quashed several pending cases and dismissed others in terms of the settlement, effectively ending all civil and criminal litigations between the parties.
Case: Anu Bhandari vs. Pradip Bhandari
Date: 5th March 2018

---

Q: What was the primary legal issue in the case Akhilesh Singh @ Akhileshwar Singh vs. Lal Babu Singh & Ors.?
A: The primary legal issue was whether the High Court erred in allowing additional evidence in the First Appeal without giving the appellant an opportunity to rebut or explain the additional evidence, which led to the setting aside of the trial court's decree in a partition suit.
Case: Akhilesh Singh @ Akhileshwar Singh vs. Lal Babu Singh & Ors.
Date: 21st February 2018

---

Q: What instructions did the Supreme Court give to the High Court for reconsidering the First Appeal in the case Akhilesh Singh @ Akhileshwar Singh vs. Lal Babu Singh & Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court instructed the High Court to decide the First Appeal afresh, giving the appellant an opportunity to lead evidence in rebuttal or explain the alleged admissions in the additional evidence. The Supreme Court expected the High Court to conclude the process expeditiously within six months.
Case: Akhilesh Singh @ Akhileshwar Singh vs. Lal Babu Singh & Ors.
Date: 21st February 2018

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court address the timing of the High Court's decision on additional evidence in the case Akhilesh Singh @ Akhileshwar Singh vs. Lal Babu Singh & Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court noted that the High Court simultaneously admitted additional evidence and decided the First Appeal on the same day, without providing the appellant an opportunity to respond to the new evidence, which was a procedural irregularity.
Case: Akhilesh Singh @ Akhileshwar Singh vs. Lal Babu Singh & Ors.
Date: 21st February 2018

---

Q: What was the broader implication of the Supreme Court's judgment in Vikash Kumar's case?
A: The broader implication of the judgment was the affirmation of the rights of persons with disabilities to reasonable accommodations in competitive examinations, reinforcing the principle of non-discrimination and equal opportunity.
Case: Vikash Kumar vs. Union Public Service Commission & Ors.
Date: 11th February 2021

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court say about the relevance of the 'first degree nexus' in the context of Section 80-IB?
A: The Supreme Court reiterated that for profits to be eligible for deductions under Section 80-IB, they must have a 'first degree nexus' with the industrial undertaking. Profits from Duty Drawback and DEPB schemes were deemed to have an indirect nexus and thus not eligible.
Case: M/s. Saraf Exports vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, Jaipur-III
Date: 10th April 2023

---

Q: What was the Oversight Committee's (OC) opinion regarding the deficiencies noted by the MCI?
A: The OC found that the deficiencies were within acceptable limits, noting that some staff were on leave due to the Diwali festival and others arrived late. The OC's opinion was that there were no significant deficiencies, and it confirmed the Letter of Permission (LOP) for the college.
Case: World College of Medical Sciences & Research and Hospital vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 5th September 2017

---

Q: What was the main issue in the case Avtar Singh vs. Union of India and Ors.?
A: The main issue was whether the termination of Avtar Singh from service in the CRPF for not disclosing his involvement in a criminal case was justified.
Case: Avtar Singh vs. Union of India and Ors.
Date: 15th November 2017

---

Q: Why was Avtar Singh terminated from service in the CRPF?
A: Avtar Singh was terminated from service for suppressing the fact that he was involved in a criminal case when he filled out the verification form during his appointment process.
Case: Avtar Singh vs. Union of India and Ors.
Date: 15th November 2017

---

Q: What were the charges in the criminal case against Avtar Singh?
A: Avtar Singh was charged under Sections 323, 324 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
Case: Avtar Singh vs. Union of India and Ors.
Date: 15th November 2017

---

Q: What was the outcome of the criminal case against Avtar Singh?
A: Avtar Singh was acquitted by the trial court on 2nd May 1994, but an appeal against the acquittal was pending at the time of his termination.
Case: Avtar Singh vs. Union of India and Ors.
Date: 15th November 2017

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court's earlier judgment in Avtar Singh v. Union of India and Others (2016) 8 SCC 471 state about disclosure of criminal cases by employees?
A: The Supreme Court's earlier judgment stated that employees must truthfully disclose any involvement in criminal cases, whether it results in conviction, acquittal, or is pending. The employer can take action based on the nature of the offense and the circumstances of the case.
Case: Avtar Singh vs. Union of India and Ors.
Date: 15th November 2017

---

Q: What direction did the Supreme Court give to the Appointing Authority regarding Avtar Singh's case?
A: The Supreme Court directed the Appointing Authority to reconsider Avtar Singh's case in light of the principles laid down in the 2016 judgment and to pass a speaking order after considering the subsequent developments in the criminal case.
Case: Avtar Singh vs. Union of India and Ors.
Date: 15th November 2017

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final ruling in the case of Shri Ram Shridhar Chimurkar vs. Union of India & Anr.?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, affirming the High Court's judgment that Shri Ram Shridhar Chimurkar, adopted by the widow of the deceased government servant after his death, was not entitled to family pension under Rule 54(14)(b) of the CCS (Pension) Rules.
Case: Shri Ram Shridhar Chimurkar vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 17th January 2023

---

Q: What did the Division Bench of the High Court decide on the appeal filed by Isha Distribution House Pvt. Ltd.?
A: The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the Single Judge's order to revoke the leave granted to the appellant.
Case: Isha Distribution House Pvt. Ltd. vs. Aditya Birla Nuvo Ltd. & Anr.
Date: 7th March 2019

---

Q: What was the primary legal issue in the case S. Nambi Narayanan vs. Siby Mathews & Others?
A: The primary legal issue was whether the wrongful arrest and prosecution of S. Nambi Narayanan, a former ISRO scientist, by the Kerala police constituted malicious prosecution and a violation of his fundamental rights.
Case: S. Nambi Narayanan vs. Siby Mathews & Others
Date: 14th September 2018

---

Q: What triggered the wrongful arrest and prosecution of S. Nambi Narayanan?
A: The wrongful arrest and prosecution were triggered by allegations of espionage involving Maldivian nationals and the alleged leak of ISRO secrets, leading to the arrest of Nambi Narayanan and others in 1994.
Case: S. Nambi Narayanan vs. Siby Mathews & Others
Date: 14th September 2018

---

Q: What was the outcome of the investigation conducted by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) regarding the allegations against Nambi Narayanan?
A: The CBI investigation concluded that the allegations of espionage against Nambi Narayanan and other ISRO scientists were false and unsubstantiated. The CBI filed a closure report, which was accepted by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, resulting in the discharge of all accused in 1996.
Case: S. Nambi Narayanan vs. Siby Mathews & Others
Date: 14th September 2018

---

Q: How did the Kerala High Court initially respond to the petition filed by Nambi Narayanan seeking action against the police officers involved in his wrongful arrest?
A: The Kerala High Court initially upheld the State Government's decision not to take disciplinary action against the police officers involved in Nambi Narayanan's wrongful arrest and prosecution, citing a lack of evidence and the passage of time.
Case: S. Nambi Narayanan vs. Siby Mathews & Others
Date: 14th September 2018

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the Kerala Government's decision not to take action against the erring police officers?
A: The Supreme Court criticized the Kerala Government's decision, stating that the wrongful arrest and prosecution of Nambi Narayanan caused immense mental agony and physical suffering. The Court highlighted the failure of the Kerala police to conduct a proper investigation and their wrongful actions against the ISRO scientists.
Case: S. Nambi Narayanan vs. Siby Mathews & Others
Date: 14th September 2018

---

Q: What compensation did the Supreme Court award to Nambi Narayanan for his wrongful arrest and prosecution?
A: The Supreme Court awarded Nambi Narayanan a compensation of Rs. 50 lakhs for the mental agony and physical suffering caused by his wrongful arrest and prosecution, directing the State of Kerala to pay this amount.
Case: S. Nambi Narayanan vs. Siby Mathews & Others
Date: 14th September 2018

---

Q: What was the main legal issue in the case Ashok Kumar & Ors. vs. The State of Jharkhand & Ors.?
A: The main legal issue was whether the mandatory requirement for judicial officers to pass a higher grade Hindi examination for confirmation and increment, as per the Bihar Civil Service (Judicial Branch) Training and Departmental Examination Rules, 1963, applied under the Jharkhand Judicial Service (Recruitment) Rules, 2004.
Case: Ashok Kumar & Ors. vs. The State of Jharkhand & Ors.
Date: 11th May 2018

---

Q: What did Rule 21(b) of the Jharkhand Judicial Service (Recruitment) Rules, 2004 stipulate regarding the confirmation of trainees?
A: Rule 21(b) stipulated that successful passing of an examination conducted by the Judicial Academy under the directions and guidance of the High Court was the only condition precedent for confirmation of the trainees as Civil Judges, Junior Division (Munsif)/Civil Judges, Senior Division (Subordinate Judges).
Case: Ashok Kumar & Ors. vs. The State of Jharkhand & Ors.
Date: 11th May 2018

---

Q: What was the High Court's position regarding the requirement of passing the Hindi examination?
A: The High Court held that passing the higher grade Hindi examination was mandatory for confirmation and increments, relying on Rule 7 of the Bihar Government Servant (Hindi Examination) Regulation, 1968, and Rule 27(a) of the Bihar Civil Service (Judicial Branch) Training and Departmental Examination Rules, 1963.
Case: Ashok Kumar & Ors. vs. The State of Jharkhand & Ors.
Date: 11th May 2018

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court interpret the applicability of the 1963 Bihar Rules under the 2004 Jharkhand Rules?
A: The Supreme Court held that the 1963 Bihar Rules could not be read into the 2004 Jharkhand Rules, as the latter were in supersession of all earlier Rules and did not explicitly require passing the higher grade Hindi examination as a condition for confirmation.
Case: Ashok Kumar & Ors. vs. The State of Jharkhand & Ors.
Date: 11th May 2018

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the mandatory requirement of the Hindi examination for confirmation?
A: The Supreme Court concluded that the 2004 Jharkhand Rules did not mandate passing the higher grade Hindi examination for confirmation, and any such prescription should have been explicitly included in the Rules.
Case: Ashok Kumar & Ors. vs. The State of Jharkhand & Ors.
Date: 11th May 2018

---

Q: What was the main issue in the case M/S. Centrotrade Minerals and Metals Inc. vs. Hindustan Copper Ltd.?
A: The main issue was the enforcement of the second-tier arbitration award made by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) in London, which contradicted the first-tier arbitration award made in India.
Case: M/S. Centrotrade Minerals and Metals Inc. vs. Hindustan Copper Ltd.
Date: 2nd June 2020

---

Q: What were the findings of the first-tier arbitration conducted by the Indian Council of Arbitration?
A: The first-tier arbitration by the Indian Council of Arbitration resulted in a Nil Award, indicating that no amount was payable by Hindustan Copper Ltd. to Centrotrade Minerals and Metals Inc.
Case: M/S. Centrotrade Minerals and Metals Inc. vs. Hindustan Copper Ltd.
Date: 2nd June 2020

---

Q: What did the second-tier arbitration award by the ICC in London decide?
A: The ICC arbitration in London awarded Centrotrade $152,112.33 for the first shipment, $15,815.59 for demurrage on the first shipment, $284,653.53 for the second shipment, $82,733 in legal costs, and $29,000 for arbitration fees and expenses.
Case: M/S. Centrotrade Minerals and Metals Inc. vs. Hindustan Copper Ltd.
Date: 2nd June 2020

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court view the discretion of State Governments in adopting UGC Regulations?
A: The Supreme Court affirmed that State Governments have the discretion to adopt UGC Regulations partially and are not bound to implement the entire scheme, including the enhanced retirement age.
Case: Dr. J. Vijayan & Others vs. The State of Kerala & Others
Date: 2nd August 2022

---

Q: What was the ruling of the Collector, Madhipura, and the Board of Revenue regarding the sale?
A: The Collector, Madhipura, set aside the Certificate Officer's order, stating that the required deposit was not made within the stipulated time. This decision was confirmed by the Board of Revenue, which dismissed the revision application of the respondent-writ petitioners.
Case: Narayan Yadav (D) Thr.Lrs. vs. The State of Bihar & Ors.
Date: 25th February 2020

---

Q: How did the High Court of Patna rule on the writ petition filed by the respondent-writ petitioners?
A: The High Court of Patna allowed the writ petition, restoring the Certificate Officer's order and setting aside the sale. This decision was confirmed by the Division Bench of the High Court in the Letters Patent Appeal.
Case: Narayan Yadav (D) Thr.Lrs. vs. The State of Bihar & Ors.
Date: 25th February 2020

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in this case?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and confirmed the order of the Board of Revenue. The application filed by the respondent-writ petitioners under Section 28 was rejected, and they were entitled to a refund of the deposited money.
Case: Narayan Yadav (D) Thr.Lrs. vs. The State of Bihar & Ors.
Date: 25th February 2020

---

Q: What was the primary legal issue in the case Shiv Developers vs. Aksharay Developers & Ors.?
A: The primary legal issue was whether the suit filed by Shiv Developers, an unregistered partnership firm, was barred under Section 69(2) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, which prohibits unregistered firms from enforcing rights arising from contracts.
Case: Shiv Developers vs. Aksharay Developers & Ors.
Date: 31st January 2022

---

Q: How did the High Court rule on the revision application filed by the contesting defendants?
A: The High Court allowed the revision application filed by the contesting defendants and reversed the Trial Court's order, holding that the suit was barred under Section 69(2) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, as it was filed by an unregistered partnership firm.
Case: Shiv Developers vs. Aksharay Developers & Ors.
Date: 31st January 2022

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's interpretation of Section 69(2) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, in this case?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted Section 69(2) as not being a bar to the suit filed by Shiv Developers, as the transaction in question was not arising out of the business of the firm but was an independent transaction of sale of the firm's share in the suit property to the contesting defendants.
Case: Shiv Developers vs. Aksharay Developers & Ors.
Date: 31st January 2022

---

Q: What were the allegations made by Shiv Developers against Aksharay Developers & Ors.?
A: Shiv Developers alleged that Aksharay Developers & Ors. had fraudulently constituted a new partnership firm under the same name and clandestinely executed a sale deed, purchasing Shiv Developers' share in the suit property without discharging the sale consideration.
Case: Shiv Developers vs. Aksharay Developers & Ors.
Date: 31st January 2022

---

Q: What was the basis of Shiv Developers' claim for the suit property?
A: Shiv Developers claimed that the sale deed executed on behalf of the firm was based on fraud and misrepresentation, and that the sale consideration was not received, making the sale deed null and void.
Case: Shiv Developers vs. Aksharay Developers & Ors.
Date: 31st January 2022

---

Q: Did the Supreme Court uphold or overturn the High Court's decision regarding the pendente lite interest?
A: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, confirming that the Arbitrator's award of pendente lite interest was not sustainable due to the express prohibition in the contract.
Case: Garg Builders vs. Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited

---

Q: What was the outcome of the first appeal filed by Kedar Nath before the Additional District Judge?
A: The Additional District Judge dismissed the first appeal filed by Kedar Nath and upheld the judgment and decree passed by the Senior Civil Judge.
Case: Rajinder Tiwari vs. Kedar Nath (Deceased) Thr. L.Rs. & Ors.

---

Q: How did the High Court of Delhi rule on the second appeal filed by Kedar Nath?
A: The High Court of Delhi allowed the second appeal filed by Kedar Nath, set aside the judgment of the first Appellate Court, and dismissed the suit filed by Rajinder Tiwari.
Case: Rajinder Tiwari vs. Kedar Nath (Deceased) Thr. L.Rs. & Ors.

---

Q: What was Satnam Singh's argument in the first appeal against the judgment dismissing Sibo's suit?
A: Satnam Singh argued that he had erected a kachha structure on the land with Banta's consent and was in occupation of that structure in his own right.
Case: Jit Ram (deceased) through LRs. vs. Satnam Singh

---

Q: What was the ruling of the High Court of Chhattisgarh in Radha Bai vs Ram Narayan & Ors.?
A: The High Court allowed the appeal filed by the respondents, confirming the judgment and decree of the Trial Court, thereby rejecting Radha Bai's claim.
Case: Radha Bai vs Ram Narayan & Ors.

---

Q: What was the High Court's decision regarding Baljit Singh's claim for compassionate appointment?
A: The High Court set aside the judgment of the First Appellate Court and restored the judgment of the Trial Court, which granted Baljit Singh's claim for compassionate appointment.
Case: Bank of Baroda & Ors. vs. Baljit Singh

---

Q: What was the outcome of the Division Bench of the High Court regarding the appeal by Electrosteel Castings Limited?
A: The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the appeal by Electrosteel Castings Limited, confirming the dismissal of the suit as not maintainable under Section 34 of the SARFAESI Act.
Case: Electrosteel Castings Limited vs. UV Asset Reconstruction Company Limited & Ors.

---

Q: What were the arguments presented by Electrosteel Castings Limited regarding the assignment agreement?
A: Electrosteel Castings Limited argued that the assignment agreement dated 30.06.2018 was fraudulent and that the assignee, UV Asset Reconstruction Company Limited, could not be considered a secured creditor since the debt was allegedly discharged under the approved resolution plan of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).
Case: Electrosteel Castings Limited vs. UV Asset Reconstruction Company Limited & Ors.

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court view the allegations of fraud made by Electrosteel Castings Limited?
A: The Supreme Court found that the allegations of fraud were made without specific particulars and seemed to be a clever drafting strategy to circumvent the bar under Section 34 of the SARFAESI Act.
Case: Electrosteel Castings Limited vs. UV Asset Reconstruction Company Limited & Ors.

---

Q: What were the facts leading to the legal dispute in Mukesh Kumar & Anr. vs. The Union of India & Ors.?
A: Jagdish Harijan, an employee of the Indian Railways, had two wives. After his death, his first wife, Gayatri Devi, sought a compassionate appointment for her stepson, Mukesh Kumar, who was born to the second wife. The request was rejected based on a Railway Board circular.
Case: Mukesh Kumar & Anr. vs. The Union of India & Ors.

---

Q: What principle did the Supreme Court affirm regarding the burden of proof in cases of wrongful termination?
A: The Supreme Court affirmed that the burden of proof lies on the employer to show that the employee was gainfully employed during the period of wrongful termination if the employee pleads that he was not employed.
Case: Pradeep S/O Rajkumar Jain vs. Manganese Ore (India) Limited & Ors.

---

Q: What was the decision of the trial court regarding Mohan Chandra Tamta's ownership claim?
A: The trial court ruled in favor of Mohan Chandra Tamta, confirming his full ownership of the property and decreeing the eviction of the defendants.
Case: Mohan Chandra Tamta (Dead) Thr. LRs. vs. Ali Ahmad (D) Thr LRs & Ors.

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in Mohan Chandra Tamta vs. Ali Ahmad?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, restored the trial court's decree, and ruled in favor of Mohan Chandra Tamta, confirming his ownership and ordering the eviction of the defendants.
Case: Mohan Chandra Tamta (Dead) Thr. LRs. vs. Ali Ahmad (D) Thr LRs & Ors.

---

Q: How did the trial court and the first appellate court rule in the case before it reached the Supreme Court?
A: Both the trial court and the first appellate court dismissed the suit for possession filed by the appellant, and their judgments were confirmed by the High Court, which dismissed the appellant's Regular Second Appeal.
Case: Kedar Nath Kohli (Dead) by LRs. vs. Baldev Singh

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in this case?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgments of the High Court, first appellate court, and trial court, and decreed the suit filed by the original plaintiff Mehar Chand Kohli, granting possession of Plot No. 27 to the appellant.
Case: Kedar Nath Kohli (Dead) by LRs. vs. Baldev Singh

---

Q: What was the High Court's decision regarding the Revenue's appeal against the ITAT's order?
A: The High Court dismissed the Revenue's appeal, affirming the ITAT's order and ruling that the appeal did not involve any substantial questions of law.
Case: Commissioner of Income Tax-I vs. M/s Rashtradoot (HUF)

---

Q: What did the Division Bench of the High Court decide regarding the Letters Patent Appeal?
A: The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the Letters Patent Appeal by order dated 21st April 2004, confirming the judgment and decree of the Single Bench.
Case: G. Saraswathi & Anr. vs. Rathinammal & Ors.
Date: 15th February 2018

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court respond to Mr. Rajiv Daiya's failure to deposit the costs imposed in the original judgment?
A: The Supreme Court issued notices and directed the Registry to proceed as per law for the recovery of costs. When Mr. Daiya continued to evade and scandalize the court, bailable warrants were issued for his production.
Case: Suraz India Trust vs. Union of India

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's stance on the conduct of Mr. Rajiv Daiya in relation to filing public interest litigations?
A: The Supreme Court emphasized that filing public interest litigations is not a birthright and criticized Mr. Daiya for using such petitions as a means to scandalize the court and evade accountability. The Court reaffirmed its earlier order barring the Trust and Mr. Daiya from filing public interest petitions.
Case: Suraz India Trust vs. Union of India

---

Q: What was the outcome of the second appeal filed by the respondents before the High Court of Uttarakhand?
A: The High Court of Uttarakhand allowed the second appeal filed by the respondents, decreeing their suit for eviction and confirming their ownership of the suit property.
Case: D. N. Joshi (D) Thr. LRs. & Others vs. D.C. Harris & Another
Date: 3rd July 2017

---

Q: What was the main issue in the case of Sourabh Brala & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.?
A: The main issue was the petition filed by students admitted to the first year MBBS Course at Respondent No. 5 College, seeking transfer to another college in the state due to the college's failure to meet required standards.
Case: Sourabh Brala & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.

---

Q: How many students were affected by the issues at Respondent No. 5 College?
A: A total of 150 students admitted to the first year MBBS Course were affected.
Case: Sourabh Brala & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.

---

Q: What was the provision for students who had completed the first year MBBS course at Respondent No. 5 College?
A: If the university granted affiliation and the Medical Council of India gave permission, the students could sit for their first year MBBS examination conducted by the affiliating university.
Case: Sourabh Brala & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court say about the capture of affirmative action benefits by ineligible individuals in this case?
A: The Court noted that the capture of affirmative action benefits by individuals who do not genuinely belong to the beneficiary groups constitutes a serious fraud on the Constitution, depriving genuine beneficiaries of their legitimate entitlements.
Case: Chairman and Managing Director FCI and Ors vs. Jagdish Balaram Bahira and Ors

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court address the issue of equities arising from the lapse of time in this case?
A: The Court examined whether equities that arise due to the passage of time could be protected under judicial review. However, the Court ultimately emphasized that fraudulent claims cannot be sustained, regardless of the passage of time.
Case: Chairman and Managing Director FCI and Ors vs. Jagdish Balaram Bahira and Ors

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's stance on retaining benefits obtained through false caste claims in this case?
A: The Supreme Court held that individuals who obtained benefits through false caste claims could not retain those benefits, as doing so would constitute a fraud on the Constitution and deprive genuine beneficiaries of their rights.
Case: Chairman and Managing Director FCI and Ors vs. Jagdish Balaram Bahira and Ors

---

Q: What was the outcome of the first bunch of writ petitions challenging the land acquisition notification under Section 4?
A: The first bunch of writ petitions challenging the notification under Section 4 was unsuccessful. The challenge was on the ground that the notification was not for a public purpose, but the High Court rejected this challenge on 15th November 1983 in a judgment reported as Munni Lal v. Lt. Governor of Delhi.
Case: Delhi Development Authority vs Sunil Khatri & Ors.

---

Q: What was the decision of the High Court of Madras regarding the provisional selection list?
A: The High Court of Madras quashed the provisional selection list and directed that the meritorious candidates should be adjusted against the general vacancies first, followed by filling the backlog vacancies and then the current vacancies under the quota.
Case: The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. vs. K. Shobana Etc. Etc.

---

Q: What was the argument of the appellants regarding the interpretation of Section 27(f) of the Tamil Nadu Government Servants (Conditions of Service) Act, 2016?
A: The appellants argued that the Section's clear provisions must be given effect, which implied that the backlog vacancies should be filled first based on merit, and then the remaining vacancies should be adjusted against the reserved categories.
Case: The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. vs. K. Shobana Etc. Etc.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's interpretation of Section 27(f) regarding the reservation and backlog vacancies?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted that the merit list should be prepared first without reservation. After that, the backlog vacancies should be filled first, followed by the current year vacancies under the reserved categories. The Court emphasized that the principle of merit should not be compromised.
Case: The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. vs. K. Shobana Etc. Etc.

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in this case?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, agreeing with the High Court's interpretation that meritorious candidates should first be adjusted against the general category, and only thereafter should the backlog and current vacancies for the reserved categories be filled. The Court left the parties to bear their own costs.
Case: The State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. vs. K. Shobana Etc. Etc.

---

Q: What was the High Court's judgment on the matter prior to the Supreme Court's involvement?
A: The High Court of Karnataka, in its judgment dated 2nd December 2014, upheld the objections of the Karnataka Co-operative Milk Producers Federation Ltd. and confirmed the order of the IPAB, which had canceled the registration of the 'NANDHINI' mark for M/S. Nandhini Deluxe.
Case: M/S. Nandhini Deluxe vs Karnataka Co-operative Milk Producers Federation Ltd.
Date: 26th July 2018

---

Q: What was the primary grievance of the appellants in the case of Shaikh Ansar Ahmad Md. Husain vs The State of Maharashtra & Ors.?
A: The primary grievance was related to the misappropriation of government funds in the implementation of the housing scheme under the Integrated Housing and Slum Development Programme (IHSDP) by the Municipal Council, Naldurg, which led to the initiation of criminal proceedings against the responsible officers and contractors.
Case: Shaikh Ansar Ahmad Md. Husain vs The State of Maharashtra & Ors.
Date: 5th October 2021

---

Q: What were the key findings of the Divisional Commissioner's report regarding the housing project?
A: The key findings included that only 302 out of 1206 planned housing units were constructed, of which 202 were usable and 100 were in a dilapidated condition. The report also highlighted excess payments made to contractors and suggested actions like recovering excess amounts, blacklisting contractors, and initiating criminal prosecutions.
Case: Shaikh Ansar Ahmad Md. Husain vs The State of Maharashtra & Ors.
Date: 5th October 2021

---

Q: How did the High Court respond to the findings and recommendations of the Divisional Commissioner's report?
A: The High Court directed the authorities to take steps in accordance with the report to their logical end, including repairing and allotting houses, recovering excess payments from contractors, blacklisting defaulting contractors, and initiating criminal prosecutions against those responsible for irregularities.
Case: Shaikh Ansar Ahmad Md. Husain vs The State of Maharashtra & Ors.
Date: 5th October 2021

---

Q: What was the final ruling of the Supreme Court in the case?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the High Court's directions for taking necessary actions to address the irregularities in the IHSDP project. The Court clarified that its observations should not preclude any arguments or defenses the appellants might present in the ongoing criminal proceedings.
Case: Shaikh Ansar Ahmad Md. Husain vs The State of Maharashtra & Ors.
Date: 5th October 2021

---

Q: What did the MCI find during the surprise inspection on 9th December 2016 at Shri Venkateshwara University?
A: During the surprise inspection on 9th December 2016, the MCI found that the campus was deserted, with no patients, doctors, or nurses present. The Dean refused to allow the inspection, citing an unauthorized holiday, which further confirmed the non-functioning state of the hospital and medical college.
Case: Shri Venkateshwara University vs Union of India & Another
Date: 1st September 2017

---

Q: What was the court's decision regarding the order dated 31st May 2017?
A: The court annulled the order dated 31st May 2017 and remitted the matter to the Central Government for fresh consideration of the materials on record, and after affording an opportunity of hearing to the petitioners' college, to deliver a reasoned decision on the issue of confirmation or otherwise of the conditional letter of permission (LOP) granted to them.
Case: Krishna Mohan Medical College and Hospital & Anr. vs Union of India and Another
Date: 1st September 2017

---

Q: What did the court ultimately decide regarding the conditional LOP granted to the petitioner college?
A: The court decided to confirm the conditional LOP granted to the petitioner college on 12th September 2016 for the academic year 2016-17. However, the court directed the Central Government/MCI to conduct a fresh inspection of the college for the academic year 2018-19 and to furnish the report to the court within eight weeks.
Case: Krishna Mohan Medical College and Hospital & Anr. vs Union of India and Another
Date: 1st September 2017

Date: 20th April 2018

---

Q: What was the primary issue in the case of Union of India & Ors. vs M. Duraisamy?
A: The primary issue was whether the punishment of removal from service imposed on M. Duraisamy for committing fraud while serving as a Postal Assistant was justified, or whether it should be modified to compulsory retirement as decided by the Central Administrative Tribunal and upheld by the High Court.
Case: Union of India & Ors. vs M. Duraisamy
Date: 19th April 2022

---

Q: What were the fraudulent activities committed by M. Duraisamy while serving as a Postal Assistant?
A: M. Duraisamy committed fraud by making fraudulent withdrawals in 85 RD accounts and non-crediting deposits in 71 RD accounts, defrauding a sum of Rs. 16,59,065/-. He was also involved in forging the signatures of depositors and making double payments for RD closures.
Case: Union of India & Ors. vs M. Duraisamy
Date: 19th April 2022

---

Q: How did the Central Administrative Tribunal and the High Court modify the punishment imposed on M. Duraisamy?
A: The Central Administrative Tribunal modified the punishment from removal to compulsory retirement, considering that M. Duraisamy had deposited the entire defrauded amount along with penal interest and had completed nearly 39 years of service. The High Court upheld this modification.
Case: Union of India & Ors. vs M. Duraisamy
Date: 19th April 2022

---

Q: What reasoning did the Supreme Court provide for restoring the penalty of removal from service?
A: The Supreme Court reasoned that the gravity of the misconduct, involving defrauding a significant amount of public money and damaging the department's reputation, justified the severe penalty of removal from service. The Court stated that merely depositing the defrauded amount and having a long service record did not mitigate the severity of the offense.
Case: Union of India & Ors. vs M. Duraisamy
Date: 19th April 2022

---

Q: How did the High Court of Madhya Pradesh rule on the appellants' challenge to the Will?
A: The High Court of Madhya Pradesh upheld the validity of the Will, affirming the decision of the Civil Court and dismissing the appellants' contention that the Will was forged.
Case: Meena Pradhan & Ors. vs Kamla Pradhan & Anr.
Date: 21st September 2023

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision in the case?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that there were no sufficient grounds to interfere with the concurrent findings of the lower courts, and confirmed the validity of the Will and the Letters of Administration issued in favor of Kamla Pradhan and her daughter.
Case: Meena Pradhan & Ors. vs Kamla Pradhan & Anr.
Date: 21st September 2023

Q: What was the basis of the High Court's decision to protect the appointments of certain employees in the earlier judgment dated 1st November 2012?
A: The earlier judgment dated 1st November 2012 protected the appointments of employees who had been confirmed in service before 28th November 2000, provided they gave an undertaking to give up their claim as belonging to Scheduled Tribes and agreed to be treated as General Category employees.
Case: Gajanan Marotrao Nimje & Ors. vs The Reserve Bank of India & Ors.
Date: 11th October 2018

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the High Court's order for the termination and recovery of benefits?
A: The Supreme Court found that the High Court was not justified in passing an omnibus order for termination and recovery of benefits, especially considering the long service of the appellants and the absence of any fraud at the time of their appointment.
Case: Gajanan Marotrao Nimje & Ors. vs The Reserve Bank of India & Ors.

Q: What preventive measures did the Supreme Court direct the State Governments to take regarding honour crimes?
A: The Supreme Court directed the State Governments to identify areas prone to honour crimes, issue directives to police for vigilance, prevent gatherings of Khap Panchayats, ensure police presence at such gatherings, and initiate preventive actions including Section 144 of the CrPC.
Case: Shakti Vahini vs Union of India and others
Date: 27th March 2018

---

Q: What remedial measures did the Supreme Court prescribe in the event of honour crimes occurring despite preventive steps?
A: The Supreme Court prescribed immediate lodging of FIRs, prompt investigation, providing security to affected couples, and possibly relocating them to safe houses. It also recommended the establishment of safe houses at district headquarters.
Case: Shakti Vahini vs Union of India and others
Date: 27th March 2018

---

Q: What was the primary issue in the case of Ex. Ct. Mahadev vs The Director General, Border Security Force & Ors.?

Case: Ex. Ct. Mahadev vs The Director General, Border Security Force & Ors.
Date: 14th June 2022

Q: How did the High Court of Delhi rule on Ex. Ct. Mahadev's plea of self-defense?

Date: 14th June 2022

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court decide regarding Ex. Ct. Mahadev's plea of self-defense?
A: The Supreme Court accepted Ex. Ct. Mahadev's plea of self-defense, modifying his conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Exception 2 to Section 300 IPC and setting him free for the period already undergone.
Case: Ex. Ct. Mahadev vs The Director General, Border Security Force & Ors.
Date: 14th June 2022

---

Q: What did the trial court and the First Appellate Court decide regarding the plaintiff's suit for specific performance?
A: The trial court refused the decree for specific performance but granted the alternative relief of refunding Rs.2,20,000/- with interest. The First Appellate Court affirmed this judgment but increased the interest rate from 6% to 14% and directed the plaintiff to hand over possession to the defendant.
Case: Babasaheb Dhondiba Kute vs Radhu Vithoba Barde
Date: 15th February 2024

---

Q: What argument did Dasanglu Pul present regarding the non-disclosure of her husband's properties?
A: Dasanglu Pul argued that according to the custom of the Mishmi tribe, only the first wife would succeed to the properties of the deceased husband, and she had no claim over the properties of her late husband, hence she marked 'not applicable' in the relevant column of Form 26.
Case: Dasanglu Pul vs Lupalum Kri

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the procedural compliance of the PILs?
A: The Supreme Court held that the procedural compliance under the Jharkhand High Court (Public Interest Litigation) Rules, 2010 was crucial and not merely directory. The non-disclosure of earlier similar efforts and the failure to approach statutory authorities first were significant lapses.
Case: State of Jharkhand vs Shiv Shankar Sharma & Ors.

---

Q: What was the primary legal issue in the case of M/S Trimurthi Fragrances (P) Ltd. vs Government of N.C.T. of Delhi?
A: The primary legal issue was whether 'Pan Masala', which contains tobacco and gutka, covered by an Entry in the First Schedule to the Additional Duties of Excise (Goods of Special Importance) Act 1957 (ADE Act), are taxable by the State under the Delhi Sales Tax Act 1975 and other related State acts.
Case: M/S Trimurthi Fragrances (P) Ltd. vs Government of N.C.T. of Delhi

---

Q: What was the conclusion of the Supreme Court regarding the taxation of 'Pan Masala' containing tobacco?
A: The Supreme Court concluded that 'Pan Masala' containing tobacco, covered by an Entry in the First Schedule to the ADE Act, could not be taxed by the State under the Delhi Sales Tax Act 1975 and other related State acts, as it falls under the exemption provided by the ADE Act.
Case: M/S Trimurthi Fragrances (P) Ltd. vs Government of N.C.T. of Delhi

Q: How did the High Court rule on the State's appeal in the case of State of M.P. vs Ghisilal?

Q: What did the Supreme Court state about the need to determine khatedari rights before seeking relief in a civil court?
A: The Supreme Court stated that the appellant must first approach the revenue court to have his khatedari rights decreed. Only after such determination by the revenue court could the appellant seek the relief of declaring the gift deed void in the civil court.
Case: Pyarelal vs Shubhendra Pilania (Minor) through Natural Guardian (Father) Shri Pradeep Kumar Pilania & Ors.

---

Q: What was the primary legal issue in the case of M/S GAIL (India) Limited vs M/S Indian Petrochemicals Corp. Ltd. & Ors.?
A: The primary legal issue was whether the clauses in the contract that allowed GAIL to levy 'loss of transportation charges' on IPCL were valid and enforceable, considering IPCL had to lay down its own pipelines as mandated by the allocation letter from the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
Case: M/S GAIL (India) Limited vs M/S Indian Petrochemicals Corp. Ltd. & Ors.

---

Q: What was IPCL's main contention regarding the transportation charges levied by GAIL?
A: IPCL contended that the transportation charges levied by GAIL were arbitrary and unfair, as IPCL was mandated to lay its own pipelines for gas transportation and did not use GAIL's pipelines. They also claimed that the charges were contrary to the Government pricing orders and sought a refund of the 'loss of transportation charges' paid.
Case: M/S GAIL (India) Limited vs M/S Indian Petrochemicals Corp. Ltd. & Ors.

---

Q: What was GAIL's defense for imposing the 'loss of transportation charges' on IPCL?
A: GAIL defended the imposition of 'loss of transportation charges' by arguing that it had made significant investments in constructing its own infrastructure (the HBJ pipeline) and needed to recover legitimate maintenance costs. GAIL also argued that both parties were public sector enterprises at the time of contract signing and that the contract reflected mutual consensus.
Case: M/S GAIL (India) Limited vs M/S Indian Petrochemicals Corp. Ltd. & Ors.

---

Q: What was the decision of the Single Judge and the Division Bench regarding the disputed clauses in the contract?
A: The Single Judge quashed the disputed clauses as being contrary to the Government pricing orders, unfair, and unconscionable. This decision was upheld by the Division Bench, which affirmed the Single Judge’s observations and ruled in favor of IPCL.
Case: M/S GAIL (India) Limited vs M/S Indian Petrochemicals Corp. Ltd. & Ors.

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court conclude about the validity of the 'loss of transportation charges' clauses?
A: The Supreme Court concluded that the clauses allowing GAIL to levy 'loss of transportation charges' were arbitrary, unfair, and discriminatory, as IPCL was mandated to use its own pipelines and not GAIL's HBJ pipeline. The Court ruled that such charges violated Article 14 of the Constitution of India, which ensures the right to equality.
Case: M/S GAIL (India) Limited vs M/S Indian Petrochemicals Corp. Ltd. & Ors.

---

Q: What relief did the Supreme Court grant regarding the refund of the transportation charges?
A: The Supreme Court restricted the relief to a refund of transportation charges paid within three years prior to the filing of the writ petition by IPCL. The Court ordered that the refund should be made within two months from the judgment date, failing which it would carry an interest of 8% per annum.
Case: M/S GAIL (India) Limited vs M/S Indian Petrochemicals Corp. Ltd. & Ors.

---

Q: How did the High Court rule on the writ petition filed by the Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation?
A: The High Court dismissed the writ petition and directed the MSRTC to pay back wages to the respondent from 1st November 2003 to 31st May 2018, in addition to confirming the Industrial Court's order of reinstatement with continuity of service.
Case: Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation vs Dilip Uttam Jayabhay

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the acquittal of the respondent in the criminal case?
A: The Supreme Court noted that the acquittal in the criminal case did not impact the disciplinary proceedings, as the standards of proof in criminal and disciplinary proceedings are different. The Court emphasized that the Industrial Court erred in giving undue importance to the acquittal.
Case: Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation vs Dilip Uttam Jayabhay

---

Q: How did the trial court rule on Jogi Ram's suit regarding Ram Devi's limited ownership?
A: The trial court ruled that Ram Devi's limited estate could not be expanded to an absolute estate and set aside the collusive decree and lease deed, affirming that Jogi Ram would inherit the property after Ram Devi's lifetime.
Case: Jogi Ram vs. Suresh Kumar & Ors.

---

Q: What was the outcome of the second round of litigation initiated by Jogi Ram challenging the sale deeds executed by Ram Devi?
A: The trial court decreed in favor of Jogi Ram, holding that the sale deeds executed by Ram Devi were unsustainable as they violated the limited ownership rights conferred to her and reaffirmed Jogi Ram's absolute ownership after her lifetime.
Case: Jogi Ram vs. Suresh Kumar & Ors.

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court rule on the application of Sections 14(1) and 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act in this case?
A: The Supreme Court held that Section 14(2) applied as the limited estate given to Ram Devi under the Will was not a recognition of a pre-existing right but a new title, thereby affirming that Ram Devi only had a life interest and the respondents could not inherit a better title than Ram Devi.
Case: Jogi Ram vs. Suresh Kumar & Ors.

---

Q: What was the High Court's decision regarding the trial court and appellate court judgments?

Case: Executive Officer, Arulmigu Chokkanatha Swamy Koil Trust, Virudhunagar vs. Chandran & Ors.

Q: What was the significance of the Supreme Court's decision on the vested right of appeal?
A: The Supreme Court emphasized that the right of appeal is a substantive right and becomes vested when the proceedings are first initiated. This right cannot be impaired by subsequent legislation unless explicitly stated, thus protecting the appellants from the retrospective application of increased court fees.
Case: K. Raveendranathan Nair & Anr. vs. Commissioner of Income Tax & Ors.

---

Q: What was the main issue in the case of Ranjan Sinha & Anr vs Ajay Kumar Vishwakarma & Ors?
A: The main issue in this case was the applicability of laws framed by the erstwhile State of Bihar to the newly bifurcated State of Jharkhand, specifically concerning the preparation of the First Register of pharmacists under the Pharmacy Act, 1948, after the bifurcation.
Case: Ranjan Sinha & Anr vs Ajay Kumar Vishwakarma & Ors

---

Q: What was the argument made by the petitioners in this case?
A: The petitioners argued that the First Register of pharmacists prepared by the erstwhile State of Bihar should be deemed the First Register for the State of Jharkhand and that any subsequent registration should comply with the qualifications as per the Education Regulations, 1991.
Case: Ranjan Sinha & Anr vs Ajay Kumar Vishwakarma & Ors

---

Q: What was the stance of the State of Jharkhand regarding the preparation of the First Register?
A: The State of Jharkhand contended that it had the right to prepare a new First Register of pharmacists after its formation, and it constituted a Registration Tribunal to register all persons who possess qualifications in terms of Section 31 of the Pharmacy Act.
Case: Ranjan Sinha & Anr vs Ajay Kumar Vishwakarma & Ors

---

Q: How did the High Court of Jharkhand rule on the preparation of the First Register by the State of Jharkhand?
A: The High Court of Jharkhand ruled that the State of Jharkhand could not prepare a new First Register and that the First Register of pharmacists prepared by the erstwhile State of Bihar should be deemed the First Register for Jharkhand. It also stated that only those with qualifications as per the Education Regulations could be registered subsequently.
Case: Ranjan Sinha & Anr vs Ajay Kumar Vishwakarma & Ors

---

Q: What directions did the Supreme Court give in this case?
A: The Supreme Court directed that the First Register prepared by the erstwhile State of Bihar should be treated as the First Register for the State of Jharkhand. It allowed the bifurcation of the First Register based on territorial nexus and stated that future inclusions should be made as per Section 32 (2) of the Pharmacy Act, adhering to the Education Regulations.
Case: Ranjan Sinha & Anr vs Ajay Kumar Vishwakarma & Ors

---

Q: What was the claim of the plaintiffs in the suit?
A: The plaintiffs claimed half of the suit property, asserting that they were the rightful owners and sought confirmation of their possession and correction of the entries in the Record of Rights of 1963.
Case: Janam Singh Kudada & Anr. vs. State of Bihar & Ors.

---

Q: What was the decision of the Additional Deputy Commissioner regarding the suit?
A: The Additional Deputy Commissioner decreed the suit in favor of the plaintiffs, declaring that they had a valid right, title, and interest over the suit lands and confirming their possession. The entries in the Record of Rights in the names of the defendants were declared wrong and erroneous.
Case: Janam Singh Kudada & Anr. vs. State of Bihar & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision in this case?
A: The Supreme Court disposed of the appeal, affirming the concurrent findings of the lower courts. The Court held that the Wilkinson Rules and the Bihar Kolhan Civil Justice (Regulating and Validating) Act, 1978, were applicable and upheld the majority award of the Panchayat.
Case: Janam Singh Kudada & Anr. vs. State of Bihar & Ors.

Q: What were the significant legal questions addressed by the Supreme Court in this case?
A: The Supreme Court addressed two main legal questions: (1) Whether an Emergency Arbitrator's Award falls within the contemplation of the Arbitration Act, and (2) Whether an order passed under Section 17(2) of the Arbitration Act, in enforcement proceedings, is appealable under Section 37 of the Arbitration Act. The Court affirmed that the Emergency Arbitrator's Award is valid under the Arbitration Act and that no appeal lies against an enforcement order under Section 17(2).

Q: What was the final outcome of the appeals filed by the State of Tamil Nadu?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals filed by the State of Tamil Nadu, set aside the High Court's judgment, and dismissed the writ petitions filed by the private respondents. The decision confirmed that the land acquisition for the MRTS Railway Project was lawful and that there was no obligation to provide alternate housing sites to the displaced landowners.
Case: The State of Tamil Nadu vs. Dr. Vasanthi Veerasekaran

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's stance on the issue of bona fide transferees in the case?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals filed by SJVN Ltd. and directed that the question of bona fide transferees should be finally decided in the pending regular first appeal before the High Court. It was stated that if compensation had been paid to transferees, it should not be recovered until the appeal is decided.
Case: Rajinder Singh vs. Satluj Jal Vidyut Nigam Ltd
Date: 24th September 2018

---

Q: What was the outcome of the Civil Suit No.15/1970 and its subsequent appeals?
A: Civil Suit No.15/1970 was dismissed on merits. In the first appeal, it was withdrawn by Rajinder Singh before the Division Bench on 23.6.1986 after the disputed land was acquired by the State, and compensation was paid. The High Court allowed the withdrawal of the suit with permission to file a fresh suit if necessary.
Case: Rajinder Singh vs. Satluj Jal Vidyut Nigam Ltd
Date: 24th September 2018

Q: What was the Supreme Court's observation regarding the principle of 'fraud vitiates' in this case?
A: The Supreme Court observed that the principle 'fraud vitiates' was clearly applicable in this case and could not be ignored under the guise of the scope of proceedings under Section 18/30 of the LA Act. It emphasized that fraud cannot be allowed to perpetuate in legal proceedings.
Case: Rajinder Singh vs. Satluj Jal Vidyut Nigam Ltd
Date: 24th September 2018

Q: What incident led to the legal proceedings in the case of Santosh Devi and Ors vs. Mahaveer Singh and Ors?

Date: 9th August 2018

---

Q: What was the main legal issue in the case of Securities and Exchange Board of India vs. Kanaiyalal Baldevbhai Patel?
A: The main legal issue was whether 'non-intermediary front-running' in the securities market constitutes a fraudulent and unfair trade practice under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices relating to Securities Market) Regulations, 2003 (FUTP 2003).
Case: Securities and Exchange Board of India vs. Kanaiyalal Baldevbhai Patel
Date: 20th September 2017

---

Q: What actions were Kanaiyalal Baldevbhai Patel and Dipak Patel accused of in this case?
A: Kanaiyalal Baldevbhai Patel and Dipak Patel were accused of using confidential information about substantial trading orders from Passport India Investment (Mauritius) Ltd. to engage in trading activities before the orders were executed, thereby making profits from the subsequent price movements.
Case: Securities and Exchange Board of India vs. Kanaiyalal Baldevbhai Patel
Date: 20th September 2017

---

Q: What was the outcome of the appeals filed by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in this case?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals filed by SEBI, setting aside the orders of the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT), and restored the penalties imposed by the adjudicating authority on the respondents for engaging in fraudulent and unfair trade practices.
Case: Securities and Exchange Board of India vs. Kanaiyalal Baldevbhai Patel
Date: 20th September 2017

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court interpret the term 'fraud' under Regulation 2(c) of FUTP 2003?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted 'fraud' under Regulation 2(c) of FUTP 2003 to include any act, expression, omission, or concealment, whether deceitful or not, that induces another person to deal in securities, regardless of whether there is any wrongful gain or avoidance of any loss.
Case: Securities and Exchange Board of India vs. Kanaiyalal Baldevbhai Patel
Date: 20th September 2017

---

Q: What was the significance of the relationship between Dipak Patel and Kanaiyalal Baldevbhai Patel in the context of the case?
A: Dipak Patel, who was privy to confidential information as a portfolio manager, shared this information with his cousin Kanaiyalal Baldevbhai Patel, who then traded on this information. This relationship and the sharing of confidential information were central to the finding of fraudulent and unfair trade practices.
Case: Securities and Exchange Board of India vs. Kanaiyalal Baldevbhai Patel
Date: 20th September 2017

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court say about the necessity of proving 'mens rea' for violations under Regulations 3 and 4 of FUTP 2003?
A: The Supreme Court stated that proving 'mens rea' (criminal intent) is not an indispensable requirement for violations under Regulations 3 and 4 of FUTP 2003. The correct test is one of the preponderance of probabilities rather than proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
Case: Securities and Exchange Board of India vs. Kanaiyalal Baldevbhai Patel
Date: 20th September 2017

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's ruling in Vinod Verma's case?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed Vinod Verma's appeal, affirming the High Court's decision and the CAT's order to redraw the seniority list based on the date of joining, referencing the earlier decision in BSNL vs. S. Sadasivan and BSNL vs. S.K. Dubey.
Case: Vinod Verma vs. Union of India & Ors.
Date: 2nd April 2019

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's reasoning for dismissing the appeal?
A: The Supreme Court reasoned that the issue was already settled by the three-Judge Bench decision in BSNL vs. S.K. Dubey and reaffirmed in BSNL vs. S. Sadasivan, which established that the seniority of Sub-Divisional Engineers should be determined based on the date of joining, not the notional date of promotion, and that the ROTA rule does not apply under the 1996 Rules.
Case: Vinod Verma vs. Union of India & Ors.
Date: 2nd April 2019

Q: What was the main legal issue in the case of The State Bank of India & Others vs. P. Soupramaniane?
A: The main legal issue was whether the discharge of P. Soupramaniane from service due to his conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude under Section 324 IPC was justified under Section 10(1)(b)(i) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
Case: The State Bank of India & Others vs. P. Soupramaniane

---

Q: What was the basis for P. Soupramaniane's discharge from service by the State Bank of India?
A: P. Soupramaniane was discharged from service because he was convicted by a criminal court for an offence involving moral turpitude, specifically under Section 324 IPC for voluntarily causing hurt by dangerous weapons.
Case: The State Bank of India & Others vs. P. Soupramaniane

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's observation regarding the High Court's reasoning for setting aside the discharge order?
A: The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's reasoning, stating that the release on probation by the criminal court did not entitle an employee to claim a right to continue in service if convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude. However, the Supreme Court examined whether the offence under Section 324 IPC involved moral turpitude.
Case: The State Bank of India & Others vs. P. Soupramaniane

---

Q: What factors did the Supreme Court consider to determine if the offence involved moral turpitude?
A: The Supreme Court considered factors such as the nature of the act, the motive behind it, whether it shocked the moral conscience of society, and the circumstances of the case. The Court concluded that the offence did not involve moral turpitude.
Case: The State Bank of India & Others vs. P. Soupramaniane

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court regarding P. Soupramaniane's discharge from service?
A: The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the High Court, concluding that P. Soupramaniane's offence did not involve moral turpitude, and therefore, he should not be discharged from service. The appeal by the State Bank of India was dismissed.
Case: The State Bank of India & Others vs. P. Soupramaniane

Q: How did the first appellate court rule on the relationship between the plaintiffs and Jagan Nath?

Case: Jarnail Singh & Anr. vs. Bhagwanti (D) Thr. LRs. & Ors.
Date: 29th November 2018

---

Q: What was the High Court's decision on the second appeal filed by the plaintiffs?
A: The High Court reversed the first appellate court's judgment and decreed the suit in favor of the plaintiffs, holding that they had proven their relationship with Jagan Nath and were entitled to inherit the suit property.
Case: Jarnail Singh & Anr. vs. Bhagwanti (D) Thr. LRs. & Ors.
Date: 29th November 2018

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision regarding the appeal filed by Jarnail Singh & Anr.?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, confirming the judgment and decree of the High Court, which had decreed the suit in favor of the plaintiffs and restored the trial court's judgment.
Case: Jarnail Singh & Anr. vs. Bhagwanti (D) Thr. LRs. & Ors.
Date: 29th November 2018

Q: What was the main legal issue in the case of Anil Bhardwaj vs. The Hon’ble High Court of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.?
A: The main legal issue was whether the appellant Anil Bhardwaj was correctly deemed unsuitable for the post of District Judge (Entry Level) due to a pending criminal case under Section 498A/406/34 IPC, despite his subsequent acquittal.
Case: Anil Bhardwaj vs. The Honourable High Court of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.
Date: 13th October 2020

---

Q: What led to Anil Bhardwaj being deemed unsuitable for the post of District Judge (Entry Level)?
A: Anil Bhardwaj was deemed unsuitable for the post due to the pendency of a criminal case filed by his wife under Section 498A/406/34 IPC, as noted in his attestation form and verified by the police report.
Case: Anil Bhardwaj vs. The Honourable High Court of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.
Date: 13th October 2020

---

Q: What was the appellant's argument regarding his suitability for the post following his acquittal?
A: The appellant argued that his case for appointment should have been reconsidered following his acquittal on 18th September 2019, as he had disclosed the pending FIR in his application and had not concealed any information.

Date: 13th October 2020

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the appellant's appeal against his disqualification?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appellant's appeal, upholding the High Court's decision that the Committee's determination of his unsuitability was valid and justified based on the pending criminal case at the time of selection.
Case: Anil Bhardwaj vs. The Honourable High Court of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.
Date: 13th October 2020

---

Q: Did the Supreme Court acknowledge any impact of the appellant's acquittal on his future prospects?
A: Yes, the Supreme Court noted that the appellant's acquittal had washed away any stigma associated with the criminal case, ensuring that his future prospects were not tainted by the prior allegations.
Case: Anil Bhardwaj vs. The Honourable High Court of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.
Date: 13th October 2020

Q: What was the main legal issue in the case of State Bank of India & Ors. vs. Rajesh Agarwal & Ors.?
A: The main legal issue was whether the principles of natural justice, specifically the rule of audi alteram partem, should be read into the Reserve Bank of India’s Master Directions on Frauds before classifying a borrower's account as fraudulent.
Case: State Bank of India & Ors. vs. Rajesh Agarwal & Ors.
Date: 1st November 2022

---

Q: What were the borrowers' main contentions regarding the RBI's Master Directions on Frauds?
A: The borrowers contended that the Master Directions on Frauds violated principles of natural justice because they did not provide an opportunity for borrowers to be heard before their accounts were classified as fraudulent, leading to significant civil consequences.
Case: State Bank of India & Ors. vs. Rajesh Agarwal & Ors.
Date: 1st November 2022

---

Q: How did the High Court of Telangana rule on the principles of natural justice in relation to the Master Directions on Frauds?
A: The High Court of Telangana held that the principles of natural justice must be read into the Master Directions on Frauds, requiring that borrowers be given an opportunity to be heard before their accounts are classified as fraudulent.
Case: State Bank of India & Ors. vs. Rajesh Agarwal & Ors.
Date: 1st November 2022

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's stance on the High Court's directive for a personal hearing before classifying accounts as fraudulent?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s directive that mandated a personal hearing before classifying accounts as fraudulent, stating that it was not necessary for the principles of natural justice to include a personal hearing at the pre-decisional stage.
Case: State Bank of India & Ors. vs. Rajesh Agarwal & Ors.
Date: 1st November 2022

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court emphasize about the impact of classifying an account as fraud on borrowers?
A: The Supreme Court emphasized that classifying an account as fraud has severe civil consequences for borrowers, including their debarment from accessing institutional finance, which could lead to their 'civil death' in the business world.
Case: State Bank of India & Ors. vs. Rajesh Agarwal & Ors.
Date: 1st November 2022

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court regarding the application of natural justice principles to the Master Directions on Frauds?
A: The Supreme Court held that the principles of natural justice, including the rule of audi alteram partem, should be read into the Master Directions on Frauds, requiring that borrowers be given an opportunity to be heard before their accounts are classified as fraudulent.
Case: State Bank of India & Ors. vs. Rajesh Agarwal & Ors.
Date: 1st November 2022

---

Q: What directions did the Supreme Court give regarding the process to be followed by banks before classifying an account as fraud?
A: The Supreme Court directed that banks must provide a notice to the borrower, allow them to respond, and consider their representation before classifying their account as fraud, ensuring compliance with the principles of natural justice.
Case: State Bank of India & Ors. vs. Rajesh Agarwal & Ors.
Date: 1st November 2022

Q: Why is it necessary to provide a hearing before classifying a borrower's account as fraud under the Master Directions on Frauds?
A: Classifying a borrower's account as fraud has significant civil consequences, including preventing the borrower from accessing institutional finance and jeopardizing the business's future. Therefore, the principles of natural justice necessitate giving the borrower an opportunity to be heard before such a classification is made  .
Case: State Bank of India & Ors vs. Rajesh Agarwal & Ors.

---

Q: How did the court view the necessity of natural justice in the classification of accounts as fraud?
A: The court held that the principles of natural justice must be followed when classifying accounts as fraud because such classification entails significant civil consequences. It requires that borrowers be given a chance to explain the evidence against them and present their case before any decision is made   .
Case: State Bank of India & Ors vs. Rajesh Agarwal & Ors.

---

Q: What does Clause 8.12.1 of the Master Directions on Frauds entail for fraudulent borrowers?
A: Clause 8.12.1 of the Master Directions on Frauds debars fraudulent borrowers, including promoters and directors, from availing banking finance from various financial institutions for five years from the date of full payment of the defrauded amount. This clause is aimed at preventing those involved in fraud from accessing further financial resources &#8203;:citation[【oaicite:0】]&#8203;.
Case: State Bank of India & Ors vs. Rajesh Agarwal & Ors.

---

Q: What was the court's stance on the involvement of borrowers during the forensic audit process under the Master Directions on Frauds?
A: The court noted that mere participation of the borrower during the forensic audit process does not fulfill the requirements of natural justice. Borrowers must be given a proper hearing to explain the findings of the forensic audit report before their accounts are classified as fraud  .
Case: State Bank of India & Ors vs. Rajesh Agarwal & Ors.

---

Q: What principle did the Supreme Court highlight regarding the consideration of bail applications in The State of Orissa vs. Mahimananda Mishra?

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the settlement between the parties in the case of B V Seshaiah vs. The State of Telangana & Anr.?
A: The Supreme Court viewed the settlement as a compounding of the offence and stated that the appellants could not be convicted based on the orders of the lower courts when the parties had agreed to settle the dispute amicably or through arbitration.
Case: B V Seshaiah vs. The State of Telangana & Anr.

A: The Supreme Court cited the case of M/S Meters and Instruments Private Limited & Anr. vs. Kanchan Mehta, which held that the nature of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is primarily related to a civil wrong and is compoundable.

Date: 1st February 2023

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court say about the High Court's role in overriding the compounding of offences in the case of B V Seshaiah vs. The State of Telangana & Anr.?

Q: What was the High Court's reason for granting bail to Rahul Modi and others in the case of Serious Fraud Investigation Office vs. Rahul Modi & Ors.?
A: The High Court granted bail on the grounds that the trial court had not taken cognizance of the complaint before the expiry of the 60-day period, entitling the accused to statutory bail.

Q: What argument did the Serious Fraud Investigation Office present against the High Court's decision in the case of Serious Fraud Investigation Office vs. Rahul Modi & Ors.?

Q: What was the Supreme Court's interpretation of Section 167(2) of the CrPC in the case of Serious Fraud Investigation Office vs. Rahul Modi & Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted that filing the charge-sheet within the statutory period is sufficient compliance with Section 167(2) of the CrPC, and cognizance does not need to be taken within that period for denying statutory bail.

Q: How did the Supreme Court rule on the issue of statutory bail in the case of Serious Fraud Investigation Office vs. Rahul Modi & Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order granting bail, ruling that the filing of the complaint before the expiry of the 60-day period precluded the grant of statutory bail under Section 167(2) of the CrPC.

Q: What previous Supreme Court judgments were referenced in the case of Serious Fraud Investigation Office vs. Rahul Modi & Ors.?

Case: Serious Fraud Investigation Office vs. Rahul Modi & Ors.

Q: What did the Supreme Court conclude regarding the continuity of custody after filing of the charge-sheet in the case of Serious Fraud Investigation Office vs. Rahul Modi & Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court concluded that once the charge-sheet is filed within the statutory period, the accused continues to remain in custody of the Magistrate until cognizance is taken by the trial court, which then assumes custody for remand purposes.

Date: 7th March 2024

---

Q: What were the specific WhatsApp status messages posted by Javed Ahmad Hajam that led to the FIR in the case of Javed Ahmad Hajam vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr.?
A: Javed Ahmad Hajam posted the following messages on his WhatsApp status: 'August 5 – Black Day Jammu & Kashmir,' '14th August – Happy Independence Day Pakistan,' and 'Article 370 was abrogated, we are not happy.'
Case: Javed Ahmad Hajam vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
Date: 7th March 2024

Q: Why did the High Court dismiss Javed Ahmad Hajam's writ petition to quash the FIR in the case of Javed Ahmad Hajam vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr.?
A: The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the grounds that the other objectionable parts of the WhatsApp status could attract the offence punishable under Section 153-A of the IPC, despite ruling that celebrating Pakistan's Independence Day did not fall within its purview.
Case: Javed Ahmad Hajam vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
Date: 7th March 2024

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court interpret Section 153-A of the IPC in the case of Javed Ahmad Hajam vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr.?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted that Section 153-A requires an intention to promote feelings of enmity, hatred, or ill-will between different groups, which was not evident in Javed Ahmad Hajam's case. The Court emphasized that expressing unhappiness over the abrogation of Article 370 is a legitimate exercise of free speech.
Case: Javed Ahmad Hajam vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
Date: 7th March 2024

Q: What precedent did the Supreme Court refer to in support of its decision in the case of Javed Ahmad Hajam vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr.?
A: The Supreme Court referred to the precedent set in Manzar Sayeed Khan v. State of Maharashtra, which emphasizes that the intention to promote feelings of enmity or hatred is essential for an offence under Section 153-A, and such intention must be evident from the language used.
Case: Javed Ahmad Hajam vs. State of Maharashtra & Anr.
Date: 7th March 2024

Date: 12th March 2018

---

Q: What were the circumstances leading to the death of Brij Bhushan Tiwari in the case of Dev Kanya Tiwari vs. The State of U.P.?
A: Brij Bhushan Tiwari was found dead at his in-laws' house, and the initial postmortem indicated that the cause of death was asphyxia due to strangulation. The prosecution alleged that Dev Kanya Tiwari and her daughter Santosh Devi (deceased) had conspired to murder him.
Case: Dev Kanya Tiwari vs. The State of U.P.
Date: 12th March 2018

---

Q: What was the trial court's decision in the case of Dev Kanya Tiwari vs. The State of U.P.?
A: The trial court convicted Dev Kanya Tiwari under Section 302/34 IPC and sentenced her to life imprisonment along with a fine of Rs. 10,000, concluding that the prosecution had proven her guilt beyond reasonable doubt based on the circumstantial evidence.

Date: 12th March 2018

Q: What was the High Court's decision on the appeal filed by Dev Kanya Tiwari?

Date: 12th March 2018

---

Q: What legal principle did the Supreme Court emphasize regarding circumstantial evidence in the case of Dev Kanya Tiwari vs. The State of U.P.?
A: The Supreme Court emphasized that in cases relying on circumstantial evidence, the chain of circumstances must be complete and lead to the only conclusion of the accused's guilt, excluding any other hypothesis. The Court found that the prosecution failed to establish such a chain in this case.
Case: Dev Kanya Tiwari vs. The State of U.P.
Date: 12th March 2018

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision in the case of Dev Kanya Tiwari vs. The State of U.P.?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted Dev Kanya Tiwari, stating that the prosecution had failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt and that the benefit of the doubt should be given to the accused.
Case: Dev Kanya Tiwari vs. The State of U.P.
Date: 12th March 2018

---

Q: What broader legal principle did the Supreme Court highlight regarding the evaluation of evidence in criminal cases in the case of Dev Kanya Tiwari vs. The State of U.P.?
A: The Supreme Court highlighted that in the administration of criminal justice, if two views are possible based on the evidence, one pointing to the guilt of the accused and the other to their innocence, the view favoring the accused should be adopted to prevent miscarriage of justice.

Q: What was the primary legal issue in the case of Sagar vs. State of U.P. & Another?

Case: Sagar vs. State of U.P. & Another
Date: 10th March 2022

---

Q: What incident led to the registration of Case Crime No.164 of 2014 under Section 302 IPC?
A: The incident involved the death of Nitin, who was found in a naked position with an electric wire around his neck in Jagpal's field. The complainant, Ravinder, alleged that his son Nitin was last seen with Jagpal and Sagar before the incident.
Case: Sagar vs. State of U.P. & Another
Date: 10th March 2022

---

Q: What was the trial court's decision regarding the application under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure?
A: The trial court rejected the application, finding that the statements of the complainant (PW1) and his father (PW2) did not provide sufficient evidence to summon Sagar as an accused. The court noted that both witnesses were not eye-witnesses to the incident.
Case: Sagar vs. State of U.P. & Another
Date: 10th March 2022

---

Q: What was the High Court's order that was challenged in the Supreme Court?
A: The High Court set aside the trial court's order and directed the trial court to reconsider the application under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure within two months, allowing sufficient opportunity to the parties.
Case: Sagar vs. State of U.P. & Another
Date: 10th March 2022

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the application of Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in this case?
A: The Supreme Court emphasized that Section 319 CrPC is a discretionary and extraordinary power to be exercised sparingly. The Court found that the High Court did not properly consider the principles laid down for invoking Section 319 and set aside the High Court's order.
Case: Sagar vs. State of U.P. & Another
Date: 10th March 2022

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision in the case of Sagar vs. State of U.P. & Another?

Case: Sagar vs. State of U.P. & Another
Date: 10th March 2022

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court address the concept of 'prima facie' evidence in this case?
A: The Supreme Court noted that the evidence needed to invoke Section 319 CrPC should be more than mere probability but short of satisfaction that would lead to conviction if unchallenged. The Court found that such strong evidence was lacking in this case.
Case: Sagar vs. State of U.P. & Another
Date: 10th March 2022

---

Q: What broader legal principle did the Supreme Court highlight regarding the exercise of power under Section 319 CrPC?
A: The Supreme Court highlighted that the power under Section 319 CrPC should be exercised only when strong and cogent evidence is available from the evidence led before the court, ensuring that it is not used in a casual and cavalier manner.
