Q: What was the significance of the decision in B. Chandrika vs. Santhosh as mentioned in the judgment?
A: The decision in B. Chandrika vs. Santhosh established that a Magistrate has the power to take cognizance of an offense on a complaint or a protest petition even after accepting the final report, and the protest petition must satisfy the ingredients of a complaint before the Magistrate takes cognizance under Section 190(1)(a) CrPC.
Case: Subhash Sahebrao Deshmukh vs. Satish Atmaram Talekar and Others

Q: What was the main legal issue in the case of Ritesh Sinha vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.?
A: The main legal issue was whether a Magistrate has the authority to compel an accused to give a voice sample during the course of a criminal investigation.
Case: Ritesh Sinha vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
Date: 2nd August 2019

---

Q: What were the charges against Ritesh Sinha in the case?
A: Ritesh Sinha was accused of being involved in a scheme with Dhoom Singh to collect money from people on the promise of securing jobs in the police force.
Case: Ritesh Sinha vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
Date: 2nd August 2019

---

Q: What were the two principal questions considered by the Supreme Court in this case?
A: The two principal questions were: (1) Whether Article 20(3) of the Constitution of India, which protects an accused from being compelled to be a witness against themselves, extends to giving voice samples, and (2) Whether, in the absence of any specific provision in the CrPC, a Magistrate can authorize the recording of an accused's voice sample.
Case: Ritesh Sinha vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
Date: 2nd August 2019

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on whether giving a voice sample is protected under Article 20(3) of the Constitution?
A: The Supreme Court held that Article 20(3) does not extend to protecting an accused from being compelled to give a voice sample, as it does not involve self-incrimination in the sense of conveying personal knowledge of the accused.
Case: Ritesh Sinha vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
Date: 2nd August 2019

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court address the issue of the Magistrate's authority to compel a voice sample in the absence of specific statutory provision?
A: The Supreme Court concluded that a Magistrate has the implied power under Section 53 of the CrPC to order the taking of voice samples for criminal investigation, filling the statutory gap through judicial interpretation.
Case: Ritesh Sinha vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
Date: 2nd August 2019

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision in the case of Ritesh Sinha vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.?
A: The Supreme Court ruled that a Judicial Magistrate does have the power to order an accused to provide a voice sample for the purpose of investigation, thereby disposing of the appeals and setting the legal precedent.
Case: Ritesh Sinha vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
Date: 2nd August 2019

---

Q: How might the Supreme Court's ruling impact future investigations involving voice samples?
A: The ruling allows investigative agencies to obtain voice samples from accused persons by seeking authorization from a Magistrate, ensuring that new evidence can be gathered effectively for criminal investigations.
Case: Ritesh Sinha vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
Date: 2nd August 2019

A: The Supreme Court suggested that the standard of proof for the accused to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of the Act is 'preponderance of probabilities' and not 'beyond reasonable doubt'.

Q: What was the main issue in the case of Union of India & Anr. vs Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed & Ors.?

Case: Union of India & Anr. vs Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed & Ors.
Date: 11th January 2022

---

Q: Why was Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed transferred to India under the Repatriation of Prisoners Act, 2003?
A: Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed was transferred to India under the Repatriation of Prisoners Act, 2003, after being convicted and sentenced to 26 years imprisonment in Mauritius for possession of heroin.
Case: Union of India & Anr. vs Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed & Ors.
Date: 11th January 2022

---

Q: What was Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed's argument for reducing his sentence to 10 years?
A: Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed argued that his sentence should be reduced to 10 years in accordance with Section 21(b) of the NDPS Act, which prescribes a maximum of 10 years imprisonment for the quantity of heroin he was found with.
Case: Union of India & Anr. vs Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed & Ors.
Date: 11th January 2022

---

Q: What was the Central Government's reason for rejecting the reduction of Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed's sentence?
A: The Central Government rejected the reduction of his sentence on the grounds that reducing the sentence by 16 years would not be compatible with Section 13(6) of the Repatriation of Prisoners Act, 2003, and the agreement with Mauritius.
Case: Union of India & Anr. vs Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed & Ors.
Date: 11th January 2022

---

Q: What was the High Court's decision regarding Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed's sentence?
A: The High Court allowed the reduction of Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed's sentence to 10 years, stating that if the offence had been committed in India, the maximum sentence would have been 10 years under the NDPS Act.
Case: Union of India & Anr. vs Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed & Ors.
Date: 11th January 2022

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court decide about the High Court's judgment in this case?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, upholding the Central Government's decision to maintain the original sentence of 26 years, stating that the sentence imposed by Mauritius was binding on India.
Case: Union of India & Anr. vs Shaikh Istiyaq Ahmed & Ors.
Date: 11th January 2022

---

Q: What is the significance of Article 8 of the agreement between India and Mauritius in this case?
A: Article 8 of the agreement between India and Mauritius states that the receiving State (India) is bound by the legal nature and duration of the sentence as determined by the transferring State (Mauritius).

Date: 11th January 2022

Q: What was the main issue in the case of Maqbool vs The State of Uttar Pradesh and Another?
A: The main issue was whether an offence under Section 326A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) is attracted in an acid attack case if the injury caused is simple.
Case: Maqbool vs The State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
Date: 7th September 2018

---

Q: What is the distinction between Sections 326A and 326B of the IPC?
A: Section 326A deals with voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, which includes permanent or partial damage or deformity, burns, maiming, disfigurement, or disability. Section 326B deals with voluntarily throwing or attempting to throw acid, which includes similar injuries but does not require actual injury to have occurred.
Case: Maqbool vs The State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
Date: 7th September 2018

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court conclude regarding the application of Section 326A in this case?
A: The Supreme Court concluded that Section 326A IPC can be attracted even if the injuries caused are simple, as long as they fall under the specified types such as permanent or partial damage, deformity, burns, maiming, disfigurement, or disability.
Case: Maqbool vs The State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
Date: 7th September 2018

---

Q: What was the appellant's argument for seeking discharge under Section 326A IPC?
A: The appellant argued that since the injury caused was simple as per the medical report, he should be discharged from the charges under Section 326A IPC.
Case: Maqbool vs The State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
Date: 7th September 2018

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court say about the relevance of the nature of injury in acid attack cases under Sections 326A and 326B?
A: The Supreme Court stated that the nature of injury, whether simple or grievous, is irrelevant for distinguishing between Sections 326A and 326B IPC as long as the injury falls under the specified types mentioned in the sections.
Case: Maqbool vs The State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
Date: 7th September 2018

---

Q: What was the outcome of the appellant's appeal in the Supreme Court?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appellant's appeal, upholding the trial court's decision to frame charges under Section 326A IPC despite the injury being simple.
Case: Maqbool vs The State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
Date: 7th September 2018

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court interpret the provisions of Section 326A IPC?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted Section 326A IPC to mean that the provision applies to any of the specified injuries caused by acid attacks, regardless of whether the injuries are simple or grievous.
Case: Maqbool vs The State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
Date: 7th September 2018

---

Q: What precedent did the Supreme Court set regarding the interpretation of injury severity under Section 326A IPC?
A: The Supreme Court set the precedent that the severity of the injury (simple or grievous) does not affect the applicability of Section 326A IPC, as long as the injury is one of the types specified in the section.
Case: Maqbool vs The State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
Date: 7th September 2018

---

Q: What could be the implications of this judgment for future acid attack cases?
A: This judgment clarifies that Section 326A IPC can be applied to acid attacks causing simple injuries, ensuring stricter punishment and legal recourse for victims of acid attacks.
Case: Maqbool vs The State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
Date: 7th September 2018

---

Q: What should legal practitioners consider when handling cases involving acid attacks under Sections 326A and 326B IPC?
A: Legal practitioners should consider that the applicability of Sections 326A and 326B IPC depends on the nature of the act (use of acid) and the type of injury specified, rather than the severity of the injury.
Case: Maqbool vs The State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
Date: 7th September 2018

---

Q: What might happen if future cases involve similar facts with simple injuries from acid attacks?
A: Future cases involving simple injuries from acid attacks may see charges framed under Section 326A IPC, following the precedent set by this judgment, ensuring accountability and stricter legal measures against perpetrators.
Case: Maqbool vs The State of Uttar Pradesh and Another
Date: 7th September 2018

Q: What was the main issue in the case of Shilpa Mittal vs State of NCT of Delhi & Anr.?
A: The main issue was whether an offense prescribing a maximum sentence of more than 7 years imprisonment but not providing any minimum sentence, or providing a minimum sentence of less than 7 years, can be considered a 'heinous offense' under Section 2(33) of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015.
Case: Shilpa Mittal vs State of NCT of Delhi & Anr.
Date: 9th January 2020

---

Q: What was the factual background of the case?
A: A juvenile 'X' allegedly committed an offense under Section 304 of the IPC, punishable with a maximum of life imprisonment or up to 10 years and fine. The juvenile was above 16 years but below 18 years at the time of the occurrence.
Case: Shilpa Mittal vs State of NCT of Delhi & Anr.
Date: 9th January 2020

---

Q: What was the Delhi High Court's ruling on the juvenile's case?
A: The Delhi High Court ruled that since no minimum sentence is prescribed for the offense, it did not fall within the ambit of Section 2(33) of the Juvenile Justice Act, and thus the juvenile should not be tried as an adult.
Case: Shilpa Mittal vs State of NCT of Delhi & Anr.
Date: 9th January 2020

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's conclusion on the interpretation of 'heinous offense' under the Juvenile Justice Act?
A: The Supreme Court concluded that an offense not providing a minimum sentence of 7 years cannot be treated as a 'heinous offense' under Section 2(33) of the Juvenile Justice Act. However, it directed that offenses falling in the fourth category (maximum sentence more than 7 years but no minimum or less than 7 years) should be treated as 'serious offenses' until the Parliament addresses the issue.
Case: Shilpa Mittal vs State of NCT of Delhi & Anr.
Date: 9th January 2020

---

Q: What impact does this judgment have on the categorization of juvenile offenses?

Q: What was the main issue in the case of State of Rajasthan vs Gurbachan Singh & Others?
A: The main issue was whether Gurbachan Singh was correctly acquitted by the High Court under Section 302 IPC, given the evidence suggesting he shared a common intention with other co-accused in the murder of Teja Singh.
Case: State of Rajasthan vs Gurbachan Singh & Others
Date: 7th December 2022

---

Q: What were the charges against Gurbachan Singh and the other accused?
A: Gurbachan Singh and the other accused were charged under Sections 302, 324, 323, and 148 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the murder of Teja Singh and injuries caused to Harbhajan Singh.
Case: State of Rajasthan vs Gurbachan Singh & Others
Date: 7th December 2022

---

Q: What was the factual background of the case?
A: The dispute involved a land partition issue between Teja Singh and the accused. On 6th November 2000, after an altercation, the accused, armed with various weapons, attacked Teja Singh, resulting in his death, and injured Harbhajan Singh.
Case: State of Rajasthan vs Gurbachan Singh & Others
Date: 7th December 2022

---

Q: What was the High Court's decision regarding Gurbachan Singh's conviction?
A: The High Court acquitted Gurbachan Singh under Section 302 IPC, convicting him only under Section 323 IPC for causing injuries to Teja Singh, reasoning that he did not share the common intention to commit murder.
Case: State of Rajasthan vs Gurbachan Singh & Others
Date: 7th December 2022

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court conclude regarding Gurbachan Singh's participation in the crime?
A: The Supreme Court concluded that Gurbachan Singh shared a common intention with the other co-accused to commit the murder, as evidenced by his participation in the attack with a 'lathi' and his continued assault on Teja Singh.
Case: State of Rajasthan vs Gurbachan Singh & Others
Date: 7th December 2022

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court view the evidence of common intention in this case?
A: The Supreme Court held that common intention could be inferred from the coordinated attack, the weapons used, and the conduct of Gurbachan Singh, establishing his liability under Section 302 IPC read with Section 34 IPC.
Case: State of Rajasthan vs Gurbachan Singh & Others
Date: 7th December 2022

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's directive regarding Gurbachan Singh's sentence?
A: The Supreme Court restored the trial court's sentence of life imprisonment for Gurbachan Singh under Section 302 IPC read with Section 34 IPC and upheld his conviction under Section 324 IPC for injuries to Harbhajan Singh.
Case: State of Rajasthan vs Gurbachan Singh & Others
Date: 7th December 2022

---

Q: What procedural directions did the Supreme Court give regarding Gurbachan Singh's surrender?
A: The Supreme Court directed Gurbachan Singh to surrender within 21 days to serve the remaining sentence. If he fails to surrender, the authorities are to take action to detain him.
Case: State of Rajasthan vs Gurbachan Singh & Others
Date: 7th December 2022

A: Rajesh was charged under Section 306 IPC for abetting the suicide of Arvind, who left a suicide note accusing Rajesh, his father Laxmi Narayan, and his sister Indera of harassment and threats related to false dowry allegations.

Date: 18th January 2019

---

Q: What did the Trial Court decide regarding Rajesh's involvement in Arvind's suicide?
A: The Trial Court convicted Rajesh, his father Laxmi Narayan, and his sister Indera under Section 306 IPC, sentencing Rajesh and Laxmi Narayan to five years of rigorous imprisonment and Indera to three years.
Case: Rajesh vs State of Haryana
Date: 18th January 2019

---

Q: What was the High Court's ruling on Rajesh's appeal?
A: The High Court dismissed Rajesh's appeal and upheld his conviction, while acquitting his father Laxmi Narayan and sister Indera based on the evidence and the suicide note.
Case: Rajesh vs State of Haryana
Date: 18th January 2019

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the evidence against Rajesh?
A: The Supreme Court found that the evidence did not warrant Rajesh's conviction under Section 306 IPC. The Court noted that there was no proximate cause linking Rajesh's actions to Arvind's suicide and that the allegations of continuous threats were not substantiated.
Case: Rajesh vs State of Haryana
Date: 18th January 2019

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court interpret the term 'instigation' under Section 107 IPC in this case?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted 'instigation' to mean that there must be a direct and proximate cause between the accused's actions and the suicide. The Court found that the evidence did not show that Rajesh provoked or encouraged Arvind to commit suicide.
Case: Rajesh vs State of Haryana
Date: 18th January 2019

---

Q: What procedural oversight did the Supreme Court find in the High Court's decision?
A: The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in convicting Rajesh while acquitting the other accused (Laxmi Narayan and Indera) despite similar allegations and evidence against all three.
Case: Rajesh vs State of Haryana
Date: 18th January 2019

---

A: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside Rajesh's conviction and sentence under Section 306 IPC, and discharged his bail bonds.

Case: Satya Pal Singh vs. State of Madhya Pradesh

Q: What was the prosecution's stance on the applicability of the proviso to Section 372 of the Cr.P.C.?

Case: State of Maharashtra vs. Surendra Pundalik Gadling & Ors.

---

Q: Can the accused in the case of State of Maharashtra vs. Surendra Pundalik Gadling & Ors. appeal the decision?
A: Yes, the accused have the right to appeal the decision to a higher court, but they must present new evidence or legal arguments to challenge the Supreme Court's ruling.
Case: State of Maharashtra vs. Surendra Pundalik Gadling & Ors.

Q: What is the significance of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, in the judgement of State of Maharashtra vs. Surendra Pundalik Gadling & Ors.?
A: The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, played a crucial role in the judgement as it provided the legal framework for prosecuting the accused for their alleged involvement in terrorist activities and unlawful acts.
Case: State of Maharashtra vs. Surendra Pundalik Gadling & Ors.

Q: What are the potential long-term consequences for the accused in the State of Maharashtra vs. Surendra Pundalik Gadling & Ors. case?

Case: State of Maharashtra vs. Surendra Pundalik Gadling & Ors.

Q: What were the charges against Selvamani and the other accused in this case?
A: The charges against Selvamani and the other accused included gang rape under Section 376(2)(g) of the IPC, criminal intimidation under Section 506(1) of the IPC, and offenses under Section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Prevention of Women Harassment Act.
Case: Selvamani vs. State Rep. by the Inspector of Police

---

Q: What was the incident that led to the filing of the FIR against Selvamani and the other accused?
A: The incident involved the gang rape of a 22-year-old woman on 27th January 2006, where the victim was forcibly taken to a secluded place, stripped, threatened, and raped by the accused.
Case: Selvamani vs. State Rep. by the Inspector of Police

---

Q: What was the initial verdict of the trial court regarding Selvamani and the other accused?
A: The trial court convicted Selvamani and the other accused under Section 376(2)(g) and 506(1) of the IPC and Section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Prevention of Women Harassment Act, sentencing them to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment and fines.
Case: Selvamani vs. State Rep. by the Inspector of Police

---

Q: What did the High Court decide regarding the appeal filed by Selvamani and the other accused?
A: The High Court dismissed the appeals filed by Selvamani and the other accused, upholding the trial court's convictions and sentences.
Case: Selvamani vs. State Rep. by the Inspector of Police

---

Q: What potential impact could the Supreme Court's decision have on future cases involving gang rape and similar offenses?
A: The decision reinforces the importance of reliable and corroborated evidence in securing convictions, even when some witnesses turn hostile, potentially leading to more stringent handling of such cases in the future.
Case: Selvamani vs. State Rep. by the Inspector of Police

Q: What directions did the Supreme Court give in the Rashidul Jafar @ Chota vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr. case?
A: The Supreme Court issued directions governing the premature release of persons sentenced to life imprisonment, emphasizing the application of the most liberalized policy for considering such cases.
Case: Rajkumar vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's observation regarding the application of the Standing Policy for premature release?
A: The Supreme Court observed that the policy should be applied uniformly and transparently, and it should be based on the legal position at the time of conviction or a more beneficial subsequent policy.
Case: Rajkumar vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh

---

Q: What were the findings regarding the handling of the 50 specific prisoners' cases brought to the court's notice?
A: The findings indicated that three prisoners were released, one was acquitted, one was released after completing the sentence, two had their premature release rejected, and the remaining cases were pending at various administrative levels.
Case: Rajkumar vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh

---

Q: What clarifications did the Supreme Court provide regarding the application of policies for premature release?
A: The Supreme Court clarified that the policy at the time of conviction should govern the consideration of each case unless a more liberalized policy is subsequently instituted, ensuring fairness and consistency in decisions.
Case: Rajkumar vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh

Q: What was the primary legal issue in the case of Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India?
A: The primary legal issue was whether the death penalty awarded to the petitioner was in contravention of procedural requirements under Section 235(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) and relevant Supreme Court precedents.
Case: Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India
Date: 25th January 2023

---

Q: What procedural argument did the petitioner raise in Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India?
A: The petitioner argued that the Trial Court did not provide a separate hearing for sentencing, which is a requirement under Section 235(2) of the CrPC, as affirmed by the Supreme Court in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab.
Case: Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India
Date: 25th January 2023

---

Q: What was the outcome of the petitioner's request for reopening the review petition in the case?
A: The Supreme Court reopened the review petition based on the precedent set in Mohd. Arif @ Ashfaq v. The Registrar, Supreme Court of India, which held that death sentence review petitions must be heard orally by a three-Judge Bench.
Case: Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India
Date: 25th January 2023

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court address the procedural impropriety argument in Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India?
A: The Supreme Court acknowledged the procedural impropriety but held that conducting the hearing for sentencing on the same day as the conviction did not necessarily vitiate the trial, provided the accused had sufficient time to furnish evidence relevant to sentencing and mitigation.
Case: Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India
Date: 25th January 2023

---

Q: What was the petitioner's second argument regarding the death sentence?
A: The petitioner argued that the death sentence was contrary to the ratio of the Supreme Court's decision in Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India, which emphasized the need for careful consideration and adequate hearing before awarding a death sentence.
Case: Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India
Date: 25th January 2023

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the petitioner's sentence in Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India?
A: The Supreme Court upheld the death sentence, finding that the procedural requirements had been sufficiently met and that the petitioner had been given an adequate opportunity to present relevant evidence.
Case: Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India
Date: 25th January 2023

---

Q: What precedent did the Supreme Court rely on to permit the reopening of the review petition in Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India?
A: The Supreme Court relied on the precedent set in Mohd. Arif @ Ashfaq v. The Registrar, Supreme Court of India, which allowed the reopening of review petitions in death sentence cases where review petitions had been dismissed by circulation.
Case: Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India
Date: 25th January 2023

---

Q: What impact did the decision in Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India have on the procedural requirements for death sentence cases?
A: The decision reinforced the requirement for a separate and adequate hearing for sentencing in death penalty cases, ensuring compliance with Section 235(2) of the CrPC and relevant Supreme Court precedents.
Case: Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India
Date: 25th January 2023

---

Q: What clarification did the Supreme Court provide regarding the timing of sentencing hearings in death penalty cases?
A: The Supreme Court clarified that while a bifurcated hearing for conviction and sentencing is preferable, conducting the sentencing hearing on the same day as the conviction does not automatically vitiate the trial, provided the accused has adequate time to present mitigating evidence.
Case: Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India
Date: 25th January 2023

---

Q: Predictive: How might future death penalty cases be affected by the decision in Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India?
A: Future death penalty cases will likely require strict adherence to the procedural requirements of Section 235(2) of the CrPC, with a focus on ensuring that the accused has adequate time and opportunity to present evidence relevant to sentencing and mitigation.
Case: Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India
Date: 25th January 2023

---

Q: Predictive: What procedural changes might courts implement to comply with the Supreme Court's decision in Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India?
A: Courts might implement procedural changes such as scheduling separate hearings for sentencing after conviction, ensuring that the accused has sufficient time to gather and present evidence relevant to sentencing and mitigation, in compliance with the Supreme Court's directives.

Q: What was the primary legal issue in the case of V. Senthil Balaji v. The State Represented by Deputy Director and Ors.?
A: The primary legal issue was the challenge to the orders passed by the majority of the Judges when a reference was made on a difference of opinion by the Division Bench of the Madras High Court, while dealing with a Writ Petition seeking a writ of Habeas Corpus following an arrest under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.
Case: V. Senthil Balaji v. The State Represented by Deputy Director and Ors.

---

Q: What procedural argument did the appellant raise in V. Senthil Balaji v. The State Represented by Deputy Director and Ors.?
A: The appellant argued that the Enforcement Directorate had no authority to seek police custody under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and that the arrest and subsequent remand were illegal and procedurally flawed.
Case: V. Senthil Balaji v. The State Represented by Deputy Director and Ors.

---

Q: What precedent did the Supreme Court rely on to support its decision in the case?
A: The Supreme Court relied on the precedent set in the case of Directorate of Enforcement v. Deepak Mahajan, which affirmed the authority of the Enforcement Directorate to seek custody for interrogation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.
Case: V. Senthil Balaji v. The State Represented by Deputy Director and Ors.

---

Q: What procedural changes might enforcement agencies implement following this decision?
A: Enforcement agencies might implement procedural changes such as ensuring detailed documentation and compliance with all statutory requirements for arrest and remand under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, to avoid legal challenges.
Case: V. Senthil Balaji v. The State Represented by Deputy Director and Ors.

---

Q: What was the outcome of the appellant's bail application in this case?
A: The appellant's bail application was dismissed by the learned Principal Sessions Judge, and this decision was upheld by the Supreme Court, finding that the procedural and statutory requirements for remand and custody were met.
Case: V. Senthil Balaji v. The State Represented by Deputy Director and Ors.
